title: Carrier Lemma
body_md:
Let $K$ be a simplicial complex with geometric realization $|K|$. Let $X$ be a topological space with a `contractible carrier' for $K$, meaning a family of contractible subsets $(X^\sigma \mid \sigma \in K)$ indexed by the simplices of~$K$, which is monotone in the sense that $\sigma \leqslant \tau$ implies $X^\sigma \subseteq X^\tau$. Then:

    \quad
    (1) There exists a continuous map $f : |K| \to X$ with $f(|\sigma|) \subseteq X^{\sigma}$ for all $\sigma \in K$. 
    
    \quad
    (2) Any two such maps are homotopic through a family of other such maps.

    \noindent
    Thus there is a canonically specified homotopy class of maps $|K| \to X$ in this situation.

title: Carrier Lemma
body_md:
Let $\phi: P \to Q$ be a map of finite posets. Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces with monotone families of subsets $(X^p)$, $(Y^q)$ indexed by $P,Q$ respectively.
     
    Suppose the family $(X^p)$ is separated (Section~\ref{subsec:separated}) and link-cofibrant (Section~\ref{subsec:link-cofibrant}). Suppose that the subsets $Y^q$ are contractible. Then there is a unique homotopy class of continuous maps $f : X \to Y$ with the property that $f(X^p) \subseteq Y^{\phi(p)}$ for all~$p$.

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{$P$-system in~$X$} is a family $(X^p)$ of subsets of~$X$, indexed by the elements of~$P$, which is monotone in the sense that $p \leqslant p'$ implies $X^p \subseteq X^{p'}$.
 
We extend the notation to write
 
\[
X^A = \bigcup_{a \in A} X^a
\]
 
for subsets $A \subseteq P$. This captures the notion of the region `covered' by~$A$.
 
Note that $X^A = X^{{\downarrow}{A}}$ by monotonicity, and in particular $X^p = X^{\mathrm{Cone}(p)}$.
 
We do not require $X^P = X$, meaning that the sets $(X^p)$ are not required to cover~$X$.

label: ex:CW-P-system
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:CW-P-system}
    Let $X$ be a CW-complex, with open cells $(e_\alpha)$ indexed by a set $A$. Write $\overline{e_\alpha}$ for the closure of $e_\alpha$; this is the image of a closed disk $D_{\alpha}$ under a continuous map~$\Phi_{\alpha}$ called the `characteristic map' \cite[Appendix]{Hatcher_2002}.
     
    The transitive closure of the relation
    \[
    \overline{e_\alpha} \cap e_\beta \ne \varnothing
    \quad \Rightarrow \quad
    \beta \leqslant \alpha
    \]
    defines a poset structure on~$A$.
    Then
    \[
    X^{\alpha}
    = \bigcup_{\beta \leqslant \alpha} e_\beta
    = \bigcup_{\beta \leqslant \alpha} \overline{e_\beta}
    \]
    defines an $A$-system of subcomplexes of~$X$.
     
    We call this the \emph{face system} in~$X$, generalizing Example~\ref{ex:simplicial-P-system}.
     
    If $X$ is a normal CW-complex, meaning that every cell-closure is a subcomplex, then
    \[
    X^\alpha = \overline{e_\alpha}
    \]
    is a simpler equivalent definition.
     
    If $X$ is a regular CW-complex, meaning that $\Phi_\alpha : D_{\alpha} \to \overline{e_\alpha}$ is a homeomorphism for all~$\alpha$, then it is a normal CW-complex \cite[Chapter~III, Theorem~2.1]{Lundell_Weingram_1969} so the simpler definition applies in this case.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:poset-system-maps}
Here are some immediate examples.

                   
           
(1)
    A poset map $\phi : P \to Q$ is a $\phi$-map for the tautological poset systems.
    
              
           
(2)
    Let $K,L$ be simplicial complexes on vertex sets $I,J$. A simplical map $K \to L$, defined as a map $\alpha : I \to J$ between vertex sets, induces a poset map $\phi_\alpha : K \to L$ by setting $\phi_\alpha(\sigma) = \alpha(\sigma)$, the image of the set~$\sigma$ under $\alpha$.
     
    The geometric realization $|\alpha| : |K| \to |L|$ is a $\phi_\alpha$-map with respect to the face systems on $|K|, |L|$. 

              
           
(3)
    Let $(X^p)$, $(Y^q)$ be $P, Q$ systems. Let $(X^p \times Y^q)$ be the product $(P\times Q)$-system.
     
    Let
     
    \begin{align*}
        \pi_P : & \xymatrix{P \times Q \ar[r] & P}
        &
        \pi_Q : & \xymatrix{P \times Q \ar[r] & Q}
        \\
        \pi_X : & \xymatrix{X \times Y \ar[r] & X}
        &
        \pi_Y : & \xymatrix{X \times Y \ar[r] & Y}
    \end{align*}
     
    denote the projection maps.
     
    Then $\pi_X$ is a $\pi_P$-map and $\pi_Y$ is a $\pi_Q$-map.
     
    This product system has the universal property of being the {largest} $(P\times Q)$-system on $X \times Y$ for which $\pi_X$ is a $\pi_P$-map and $\pi_Y$ is a $\pi_Q$-map.
     
                                                                                                                                         
                 

(4)
    Let $P,Q,R$ be posets. Let $(X^p), (Y^q), (Z^r)$ be poset systems on $X,Y,Z$. Suppose $\phi : P \to Q$ and $\psi : Q \to R$ are poset maps. If $f : X \to Y$ is a $\phi$-map and $g : Y \to Z$ is a $\psi$-map then $gf$ is a $\psi\phi$-map.

    X^q =
    \bigcup \,
    \{ X^p \mid p \in P, \, \phi(p) \leqslant q \}

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Quillen-fiber}
    The indexing set for the union in Example~\ref{ex:phi-pushforward} is called a \emph{Quillen (down-)fiber} for the map~$\phi$. It is a closed subset of~$P$, sometimes written:
    \[
    \phi/q
    = \phi^{-1}(Q_{\leqslant q})
    = \{ p \in P \mid \phi(p) \leqslant q \}
    \]
    Thus we may define the $\phi$-pushforward by $X^q = X^{\phi/q}$.
     
    Similarly, the \emph{Quillen up-fiber} is
    \[
    q \backslash \phi
    =
    \phi^{-1}(Q_{\geqslant q})
    =
    \{ p \in P \mid q \leqslant \phi(p) \}.
    \]
    This is up-closed, and $(X^{q \backslash \phi})$ is a ${Q}^{\mathrm{op}}$-system rather than a $Q$-system.

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume (1).
     
    Even without (1) we have
     
    \[
    X^{\varnothing} = \varnothing,
    \quad
    X^{A \cup B} = X^A \cup X^B,
    \quad
    X^{A \cap B} \subseteq X^A \cap X^B
    \]
     
    for arbitrary $P$-systems and subsets $A, B \subseteq P$.
     
    With (1) we have $X^P = X$ since each $P_x$ is nonempty.                                 
     
    Now let $A, B \leqslant P$ and consider $x \in X^A \cap X^B$.
     
    Then $x \in X^a \cap X^b$ for some $a \in A$, $b \in B$. Let $p$ be the smallest element of $P_x$. Since $a,b \in X_p$ we have $p \leqslant a$ and $p \leqslant b$ and therefore $p \in A$ and $p \in B$. Thus $x \in X^p \subseteq X^{A \cap B}$. This argument establishes $X^A \cap X^B \subseteq X^{A \cap B}$ and therefore $X^{A \cap B} = X^A \cap X^B$.
     
                                

    Assume (2) and suppose $P$ is well founded.
     
    Since $X^P = X$, every $P_x$ is nonempty and therefore has a minimal element~$p$. We show that $p$ is the smallest element. Consider $q \in P_x$. Then
    \[
    x
    \in
    X^p \cap X^q
    =
    X^{\mathrm{Cone}(p)} \cap X^{\mathrm{Cone}(q)}
    =
    X^{\mathrm{Cone}(p) \cap \mathrm{Cone}(q)}
    \]
    so some element of $\mathrm{Cone}(p) \cap \mathrm{Cone}(q)$ belongs to $P_x$. By minimality, this element of $\mathrm{Cone}(p)$ can only be~$p$. This implies $p \in \mathrm{Cone}(q)$ so $p \leqslant q$.

head: environment
name: classifying map interpretation

title: Proof
body_md:
(1)
    We show that the two operations are mutually inverse.
     
    Let $X^P$ be a $P$-complex and define $m(x) = \min P_x$. Then $x \in X^p$ iff $p \in P_x$ iff $m(x) \leqslant p$. Thus $X^p = m^{-1}(\mathrm{Cone}(p))$ so $X^P$ is the $m$-pullback of $P^P$.
     
    In the other direction,
     
    let $m : X \to P$ and define $X^P$ to be the $m$-pullback of $P^P$. Then $p \in P_x$ iff $x \in X^p$ iff $m(x) \in P^p$ iff $m(x) \leqslant p$, so $P_x = {\uparrow}{\{m(x)\}}$ and $m$ is recovered by $m(x) = \min P_x$.
    
    (2), (3) follow from the identification of smallest elements in Example~\ref{ex:separation-behaves} (4), (5).

title: Proof
body_md: For $A \leqslant P$ we have $X^A = m^{-1}({\downarrow}{A}) = m^{-1}(A)$. Thus $X^P$ is closed iff the preimage $m^{-1}(A)$ is closed for every $A \leqslant P$, that is, for every Alexandrov-closed $A \subseteq P$.

label: ex:closed
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:closed}
The following topological poset systems are closed:

    (1) The tautological system on a poset with the Alexandrov topology.

    (2) The face system on a simplicial complex or CW-complex.

    (3) Any subsystem of a closed poset system.

    (4) The product of two closed poset complexes.

    (5) The $f$-pullback of a closed poset system, for a continuous map $f$.

    (6) The $\phi$-pushforward of a closed poset system, for a poset map $\phi : P \to Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proofs of (1), (2), (3), (5), (6) are immediate. For (4), let $X^P, Y^Q$ be closed complexes with classifying maps $m : X \to P$, $n : Y \to Q$. Then $m \times n : X \times Y \to P \times Q$ is the classifying map for $X^P \times Y^Q$. Now $m,n$ are continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:cc-classifying}, so $m \times n$ is continuous with respect to the product topology on $P \times Q$. This topology is the same as the (ostensibly finer) Alexandrov topology on $P \times Q$, because every Alexandrov-open set $U \subseteq P \times Q$ is a union of product open sets:
    \[
    U
                                                       
                                                                 
    = \bigcup_{(p,q) \in U} {\uparrow}{\{(p,q)\}}
    = \bigcup_{(p,q) \in U} {\uparrow}{\{p\}} \times {\uparrow}{\{q\}}
    \]
    Then $X^P \times Y^Q$ is closed by Proposition~\ref{prop:cc-classifying}.

&
X^{\mathrm{Cone}(p)} = X^p

Consider the two-element ordered set $I = (0 < 1)$. 
 
Define $[0,1]^I$ by $[0,1]^0 = \{0\}$ and $[0,1]^1 = [0,1]$.
 
Let $C \subseteq [0,1]$ be any closed subset whose inclusion is not a cofibration, such as the Cantor set, and define $X^I$ by $X^0 = C$ and $X^1 = [0,1]$. title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x \in X$. Since $X = X^P = X^A \cup X^B$ it follows that $P_x$ must meet at least one of $A,B$.
     
    If $P_x$ meets $A$ but not~$B$, then $P_x = P_x \cap A = A_x$ which has a smallest element. If $P_x$ meets $B$ but not~$A$, then $P_x = P_x \cap B = B_x$ which has a smallest element. Otherwise $P_x$ meets both $A$ and $B$, so $x \in X^A \cap X^B = X^N$ and therefore $P_x$ meets $N$.
     
    It follows that the smallest element of $P_x \cap A$ belongs to $N$, as does the smallest element of $P_x \cap B$, so both of these smallest elements must be the smallest element of $P_x \cap N$. Since $P = A \cup B$, this is then the smallest element of $P_x$.
     
    We have shown that every $P_x$ has a smallest element.

    X^P
    = Y^A \cup_{f} Z^B
    = \big( Y^A \sqcup Z^B \big)
    \big/ \big( y \sim f(y) \mid y \in Y^N \big)

\label{thm:carrier}
Assume the following hypotheses:

    \begin{itemize}
        \item
        Let $\phi : P \to Q$ be a poset map, with $P$ finite.

        \medskip
        \item
        Let $X^P$ be a link-cofibrant $P$-complex on a topological space $X$.

        \medskip
        \item
        Let $(Y^q)$ be a cellular $Q$-system in a topological space~$Y$.

    Given a closed subset $A \leqslant P$ (possibly empty) and a continuous $\phi|_A$-map $f_A : X^A \to Y$:

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
        There exists a continuous $\phi$-map $f : X \to Y$ extending $f_A$.

        \medskip
        \item 
        Any two such extensions are $\phi$-homotopic relative to $X^A$.

    \end{enumerate}

    	\ar[u]
    }
\]
head: environment
name: Extension Lemma

title: Proof
body_md: Since $W$ is contractible, the map $f$ is homotopic to a map $c_U : U \to W$ that takes a constant value~$c$. Extend this trivially to the constant map $c_V: V \to Y$. Use the homotopy extension property to extend the homotopy $c_U \simeq f$ on~$U$ to a homotopy $c_V \simeq g$ on~$V$. The map $g$ is the required extension.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) We construct an extension cell by cell. We first extend from $A$ to $A \cup \{p\}$ where $p$ is a minimal element of $P - A$.
     
    The space $X^{A \cup \{p\}}$ is the union $X^A \cup X^p$ of two closed subspaces,
     
    and $f$ is already defined on $X^A$, so it remains to define $f$ on $X^p$ so that it agrees on the intersection, which is
     
            
    \[
    X^A \cap X^p
    = X^A \cap X^{\mathrm{Cone}(p)}
    = X^{A \cap \mathrm{Cone}(p)}
    = X^{\mathrm{Link}(p)}
    \]
    by separation and the minimality of~$p$.
     
    The task is reduced to following extension problem:
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    X^p
	   \ar@{.>}[r]             
    &
    Y^{\phi(p)}
    \\
    X^{\mathrm{Link}(p)}
    	\ar[ur]
    	\ar[u]
    }
    \]
     
    Since $X^{\mathrm{Link}(p)} \to X^p$ is a cofibration and $Y^{\phi(p)}$ is contractible, a continuous extension is provided by Extension Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}. 
     
    We extend to all of $X^P$ by repeating this process finitely many times.
    
    (2) This is a special case of (1) in the following way. Let $f,g$ be the two extensions. Write
     
    \begin{alignat*}{2}
        &R &&= P \times [0,1]
        \\
        &Z^R &&= X^P \times [0,1]^{\Delta_1}
        \\
        &B
        &&=
        (P \times \partial \Delta_1)
        \;\cup\;
        (A \times \Delta_1)
    \end{alignat*}
     
    and define $\Phi : R \to Q$ by
    $
    \Phi(p,\sigma) = \phi(p)
    $.
     
    Here $Z^R$ is link-cofibrant, being a product of link-cofibrant poset complexes.
     
    Define $f_{B}: Z^B \to Y$ by the following piecewise formula on two overlapping open subsets:
    \[
    f_{B}(x,t)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        f(x) & \text{for $t \in [0,1)$}
        \\
        g(x) & \text{for $t \in (0,1]$}
    \end{cases}
    \]
    This is consistent on the intersection $X^A \times (0,1)$ because $f(x) = g(x) = f_A(x)$ on $X^A$, so we get a continuous map $f_B : Z^B \to Y$ which is a $\Phi|_{B}$-map because $f, g$ are $\phi$-maps.
     
    The extension to a ${\Phi}$-map $Z^R \to Y$ provided by (1) is the homotopy we seek.

title: Remark
body_md: In the original Carrier Lemma~\cite{Walker_1981} where the domain is a simplicial complex, the proof of (2) is very similar to the proof of (1) but doesn't quite reduce to it, so the steps have to be written out again. Our framework has products, and the lemma is formulated in terms of extending a partially defined map, so we get (2) directly from (1).

label: lem:contractibility
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:contractibility}
    Let $M$ be a topological space and $L \subseteq M$ be a closed subspace whose inclusion map is a cofibration. In the situation of Theorem~\ref{thm:contractibility}, any continuous map $g : L \to \mathrm{Map}_\phi(X,Y; f_A)$ can be extended to a continuous map $M \to \mathrm{Map}_\phi(X,Y; f_A)$:
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    M
        \ar@{.>}[dr]^{\exists}
    \\
    L
        \ar[u]
        \ar[r]_-g
    &
    \mathrm{Map}_\phi(X,Y; f_A)
    }
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the exponential adjunction map for topological spaces
\[
\xymatrix{
\mathrm{Map}(W \times X, Y)
    \ar[r]
&
\mathrm{Map}(W, \mathrm{Map}(X,Y))
}
\]
is a bijection
 
when $X$ is locally compact (\cite[Chapter 7, Corollary 5.4]{Munkres_1984}; stated for locally compact Hausdorff but the proof does not use Hausdorff).
 
This allows us to recast the extension problem in the following form
\[
    \xymatrix{
    M \times X
        \ar@{.>}[dr]^{\exists}
    \\
    L \times X
        \ar[u]
        \ar[r]_-{G}
    &
    Y
    }
\]
with appropriate restrictions on the maps to~$Y$. Here $G(\ell,x) = [ g(\ell) ](x)$.

Let $I = (0 < 1)$ be the two-element ordered set. Then $M^0 = L$, $M^1 = M$ defines $M^I$ as a link-cofibrant $I$-complex and the product $M^I \times X^P$ as a link-cofibrant $(I \times P)$-complex.

To construct the desired extension, we apply the Carrier Lemma with the following set-up.
 
Let $B = \{0\} \times P \;\cup\; I \times A  \leqslant I \times A$.
 
Let $\Phi = \phi \circ \mathrm{proj}_P : I \times P \to Q$.
 
Let $F_B : (M \times X)^B \to Y^Q$ be the continuous $\Phi|_B$-map defined piecewise on two closed subspaces as follows:
 
\[
F(m,x)
=
\begin{cases}
    G(m,x) &\text{if $m \in L$}
    \\
    f_A(x) &\text{if $x \in X^A$}
\end{cases}
\]
 
Any extension to a continuous $\Phi$-map $F : M^I \times X^P \to Y^Q$ has the properties we seek.

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:contractibility} with $L = \mathrm{Map}_\phi(X,Y; f_A)$, with $g$ the identity map, and with $M$ the cone on $L$ (compare Proposition~\ref{prop:ccce}).

label: construction:order
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{construction:order}
    Let
    \[
        X = |\mathrm{ord}(P)|
    \]
    be the geometric realization of the order complex of~$P$. Define a $P$-system by
    \[
        X^p = |\mathrm{ord}(\mathrm{Cone}(p))|.
    \]
 
              
    To show that $(X^p)$ is separated, let $|\sigma|$ be the unique geometric simplex that contains a given point $x$ in its interior. We have $x \in X^p$ iff $\sigma \in \mathrm{ord}(\mathrm{Cone}(p))$ iff $\max(\sigma) \leqslant p$, so $P_x$ has smallest element $\max(\sigma)$ as required. Each $X^p$ is a geometric cone and a simplicial subcomplex, so $X^P$ is cellular and link-cofibrant.
            
Thus $X^P = |\mathrm{ord}(P)|^P$ is a CL-complex.

Then $|\phi|$ is a $\phi$-map with respect to the `cone' CL-complex structures on $|\mathrm{ord}(P)|$, $|\mathrm{ord}(Q)|$ defined in Construction~\ref{construction:order}.

title: Proof
body_md:

    $
    |\phi|(|\mathrm{Cone}(p)|)
    \subseteq
    |\mathrm{Cone}(\phi(p))|
    $ by the functoriality of the order complex.

label: thm:existence
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:existence}
    Let $P$ be a finite poset, let $A \leqslant P$, and let $Y^A$ be a CL-complex. Then there exists a CL-complex $X^P$ that extends $Y^A$ in the sense that the construction comes with an isomorphism $Y^A \to X^A$ of topological $A$-complexes. If $Y^A$ is compact or Hausdorff or both, we can construct $X^P$ to be compact or Hausdorff or both.
head: environment
name: existence

title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume $A \ne P$. Let $p$ be a minimal element of $P-A$, and write $B = \mathrm{Cone}(p)$ and $N = A \cap B = \mathrm{Link}(p)$.
     
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:ccce}, there exists a closed cofibrant inclusion $f : Y^{N} \to Z$, for some contractible space~$Z$. Define $Z^b = f(Y^b)$ for $b \in N$, and $Z^p = Z$. Then $Z^B$ is a CL-complex, with $f$ restricting to an isomorphism $Y^N \to Z^N$ of topological $N$-complexes. By Proposition~\ref{prop:gluing-topological} (topological attachment) the space
     
    \[
    X^{A \cup B}
    =
    Y^A \cup_f Z^B
    \]
     
    has the structure of a CL-complex for $A \cup B = A \cup \{p\}$.
     
    Repeat until done.
 
    The `compact or Hausdorff or both' assertion follows from Propositions \ref{prop:ccce} and~\ref{prop:gluing-topological}.

label: construction:iterative
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{construction:iterative}
    Let $X^A$ be a CL-complex for some $A \leqslant P$.
     
    Let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ list the elements of $P-A$ in a sequence that is non-decreasing with respect to the partial order. Let $A_k = A \cup \{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$ with $A_0 = A$. Iteratively, set
    \[
    X^{p_k} = Z_k,
    \quad
    X^{A_{k}} = X^{A_{k-1}} \cup_{f_k} X^{p_k} 
    \]
    where $f_k, Z_k$ are chosen such that
    $
    f_k : X^{\mathrm{Link}(p_k)} \to Z_k
    $
    is a closed cofibrant inclusion into a contractible space.
     
    Then $X^P$ is a CL-complex.

label: ex:lazy-sc
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:lazy-sc}
    Let $K$ be a simplicial complex on a finite set~$I$.
     
    Thinking of it as a poset $K \leqslant \Delta(I)$,
     
    we construct a CL-complex $X^K$ as lazily as possible. The minimal elements are the singleton sets\footnote{ 
    For this example we use square brackets to delimit the list of distinct elements of a subset.}
    $[a]$, so the $X^{[a]}$ must be disjoint contractible sets. The lazy choice is to make them singletons. For $\sigma \in K$, we require $X^\sigma$ to be contractible and contain $X^{[a]}$ for all $a \in \sigma$. The lazy choice is to take the convex hull. This leads to the following construction. Identify $I$ with an affinely independent subset of a real vector space. For each $\sigma = [a_0, a_1, \dots, a_k] \in K$, define:
    \[
    X^\sigma
    = \mathrm{conv}(a_0 , a_1, \dots, a_k)
    = a_0 \star a_1 \star \dots \star a_k
    \]
    Through pure indolence we have recovered the face complex $|K|^K$ of the simplicial complex.

The barycentric subdivision homeomorphism $|\mathrm{ord}(K)| \to |K|$ carries $|\mathrm{ord}(\mathrm{Cone}(\sigma))|$ to the geometric simplex~$|\sigma|$, so that $\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}(K) = |\mathrm{ord}(K)|^K$ and $|K|^K$ are topologically isomorphic CL-complexes.

We are free to understand it to mean the homotopy type of the geometric realization~$|K|$ of the simplicial complex~$K$, the homotopy type of the geometric realization of the order complex of the poset~$K$, or, in the finite case, the homotopy type of any CL-complex for the poset~$K$. label: ex:prod-complexes
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:prod-complexes}
    Let $I, J$ be finite sets and let $A \leqslant \Delta(I) \times \Delta(J)$. We can realize $A$ as a CL-subcomplex of a product of complete simplicial complexes
    \[
    |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^A
    =
    (|\Delta(I)| \times |\Delta(J)|)^A
    \leqslant
    |\Delta(I)|^{\Delta(I)} \times |\Delta(J)|^{\Delta(J)}
    \]
    with cells $|\mathrm{prod}(A)|^{(\sigma,\tau)} = |\sigma| \times |\tau|$.
     
    This object with its cell structure is called a `{prod-complex}' in~\cite{deSilva_GIRSSVY_2026}.
     
    An alternative construction produces a simplicial complex: let $\mu : \Delta(I) \times \Delta(J) \to \Delta(I \times J)$ denote the poset map $(\sigma,\tau) \mapsto \sigma \times \tau$, then
    \[
    \mathrm{simp}(A) = {\downarrow}{\,\mu(A)} \leqslant \Delta(I \times J)
    \]
    is a simplicial complex on $I \times J$, called the `{simplexification}' of~$A$. Then $|\mathrm{simp}(A)|$ admits two natural CL-complex structures: its face complex structure $|\mathrm{simp}(A)|^{\mathrm{simp}(A)}$, and the structure $|\mathrm{simp}(A)|^A$ defined\footnote{ 
    Verifying separation takes a little thought: for $x$ in the relative interior of $|\rho|$, one shows that $x \in |\sigma \times \tau|$ iff $(\sigma, \tau) \geqslant (\rho_I, \rho_J)$ where $\rho_I, \rho_J$ are the projections of $\rho$ onto $\Delta(I), \Delta(J)$.
    } by the formula
    \[
    |\mathrm{simp}(A)|^{(\sigma,\tau)} = |\sigma \times \tau|
    \]
     
    for $(\sigma,\tau) \in A$.
     
    To relate the two geometric realizations, a continuous `squashing' map
    \[
    \xi : |\mathrm{simp}(A)| \to |\mathrm{prod}(A)|
    \]
    is defined in~\cite{deSilva_GIRSSVY_2026} and shown using Smale's mapping theorem to be a homotopy equivalence.
     
    For a shorter proof (in the finite case) note that $\xi : |\mathrm{simp}(A)|^A \to |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^A$ is an $A$-map of CL-complexes and hence a homotopy equivalence.

\label{rem:inverse-functor}
 
Let $\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}(P) = |\mathrm{ord}(P)|^P$ denote the geometrically realized order complex of a finite poset~$P$ with the `cones' CL-complex structure described above.
 
Given a poset map $\phi : P \to Q$, let $|\phi| : |\mathrm{ord}(P)| \to |\mathrm{ord}(Q)|$ be the induced map. Then $\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}(\phi) = (|\phi|, \phi)$ is a CL-map by Proposition~\ref{prop:order-map}.

\xymatrix{\mathbf{fPoset} \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}} & \mathbf{CL} \ar[r] & \mathbf{hCL}}
\]
is an inverse equivalence (indeed, a strict right-inverse) to the equivalence
\[
\xymatrix{\mathbf{hCL} \ar[r] & \mathbf{fPoset}}
\]
of Proposition~\ref{prop:hCL=fPoset}.

title: Theorem

\label{thm:QTA}
Let $\phi : P \to Q$ be a map between finite posets. Suppose each Quillen fiber
 
$\phi/q = \phi^{-1}(\mathrm{Cone}(q))$
 
is a contractible subposet of $P$. Then $\phi$ is a homotopy equivalence.

name: QTA for finite posets

title: Proof
body_md: Let $X^P$ be a CL-complex. The Quillen fiber hypothesis implies that the $\phi$-pushforward $X^Q$ is a CL-complex: for cellularity, each $X^q = X^{\phi/q}$ is a CL-complex for $\phi/q$ and therefore contractible. Then the identity homeomorphism $\mathrm{id}_X : X^P \to X^Q$ is a $\phi$-map of CL-complexes (Example~\ref{ex:phi-pushforward}) so $\phi$ is a homotopy equivalence of posets.

label: thm:QTA-dual
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:QTA-dual}
Let $\phi : P \to Q$ be a map between finite posets. Suppose each Quillen up-fiber
 
$q \backslash \phi= \phi^{-1}({\uparrow}{\{q\}})$
 
is a contractible subposet of $P$. Then $\phi$ is a homotopy equivalence.
head: environment
name: QTA for finite posets, dual form

title: Proof
body_md:
The poset map $\phi : P \to Q$ is simultaneously  a poset map ${\phi}^{\mathrm{op}} : {P}^{\mathrm{op}} \to {Q}^{\mathrm{op}}$.
     
    Then ${\phi}^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a homotopy equivalence by Theorem~\ref{thm:QTA}, meaning that the geometric realization
                     
    \[
    |{\phi}^{\mathrm{op}}| : |\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}({P}^{\mathrm{op}})| \longrightarrow |\mathrm{ord}_{\textsc{cl}}({Q}^{\mathrm{op}})|
    \]
     
    is a homotopy equivalance.
     
    From the commutative diagram
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    |\mathrm{ord}(P)|
        \ar[rr]^{|\phi|}
        \ar@{=}[d]
    &&
    |\mathrm{ord}(Q)|
        \ar@{=}[d]
    \\        
    |\mathrm{ord}({P}^{\mathrm{op}})|
        \ar[rr]^{|{\phi}^{\mathrm{op}}|}
    &&
    |\mathrm{ord}({Q}^{\mathrm{op}})|
    }
    \]
    it follows that $|\phi|$ is a homotopy equivalence, hence $\phi$ is a homotopy equivalence of posets.

label: thm:gluing
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:gluing}
Suppose $X, Y$ are topological spaces with closed subspaces $X^i, Y^i$ ($i = 0, 1, 2$) such that:
    \begin{align*}
        X &= X^1 \cup X^2
        &
        Y &= Y^1 \cup Y^2
        \\
        X^0 &= X^1 \cap X^2
        &
        Y^0 &= Y^1 \cap Y^2
    \end{align*}
    Suppose $f : X \to Y$ is a continuous map that restricts to continuous maps
    \[
    f^0 : X^0 \to Y^0,
    \quad
    f^1 : X^1 \to Y^1,
    \quad
    f^2 : X^2 \to Y^2
    \]
    and suppose that these maps are homotopy equivalences.
     
    Finally, suppose that the inclusion maps
    \begin{align*}
    X^0 &\longrightarrow X^1
    &
    Y^0 &\longrightarrow Y^1
    \\
    X^0 &\longrightarrow X^2
    &
    Y^0 &\longrightarrow Y^2
    \end{align*}
    are cofibrations. Then $f : X \to Y$ is a homotopy equivalence.
    \qed

body_md:
Let $f : X^P \to Y^Q$ be a continuous $\phi$-map of CL-complexes.
     
    Let $X^R, Y^R$ denote the $\alpha$- and $\beta$-pushforwards of~$X^P, Y^Q$.
    Then $f : X^R \to Y^R$ is an $R$-map of link-cofibrant $R$-complexes. Moreover $X^r = X^{\alpha/r}$ and $Y^r = Y^{\beta/r}$ have the structure of CL-complexes for $\alpha/r$, $\beta/r$ and the restriction  $f^r : X^r \to Y^r$ realizes the induced map $\alpha/r \to \beta/r$.             
     
    By hypothesis, each $f^r$ is a homotopy equivalence, so
     
    $f$ is a homotopy equivalence by Theorem~\ref{thm:L-complex-HE}.
head: environment

label: prop:product-fiber
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:product-fiber}
    In the situation above, suppose every `point fiber' $P_q$ is contractible. Then the projection $\pi : A \to Q$ is a homotopy equivalence.
head: environment
name: product fiber theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the dual form of QTA for posets. For all $q \in Q$, the Quillen up-fiber
    \[
    q \backslash \pi
    =
    \bigcup_{q' \geqslant q} P_{q'} \times \{q'\}
    \]
    deformation retracts to the subposet $P_{q} \times \{q\}$ through the involution $(p,q') \mapsto (p,q)$. This subposet is isomorphic to $P_{q}$ which is contractible by hypothesis.
head: environment

label: prop:product-fiber-down
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:product-fiber-down}
    In the situation above, each Quillen fiber
    \[
    \pi / q
    =
    \bigcup_{q' \leqslant q} P_{q'} \times \{q'\}
    \]
    is contractible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Proposition~\ref{prop:product-fiber} for $\pi/q \leqslant P \times \mathrm{Cone}(q)$ gives $\pi/q \simeq \mathrm{Cone}(q)$ which is contractible.
head: environment

label: ex:product-fiber-CL
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:product-fiber-CL}
Let $P, Q, A, \pi$ be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:product-fiber} and suppose that $P, Q$ are finite. Let $X^P, Y^Q$ be CL-complexes, and consider the sub-CL-complex $Z^A = (X \times Y)^A$ of $X^P \times Y^Q$.
 
Certainly the $\pi$-pushforward $Z^Q$ is a link-cofibrant complex. 
 
Moreover, each $Z^q = Z^{\pi/q}$ has the structure of a CL-complex for $\pi/q$ which is contractible by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-fiber-down}. It follows that $Z^Q$ is a CL-complex, and the identity homeomorphism $\mathrm{id}_Z : Z^A \to Z^Q$ is a $\pi$-map (Example~\ref{ex:phi-pushforward}) of CL-complexes.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Since
    \[
    Z^q
    =
    \bigcup_{q' \leqslant q}
    X^{P_{q'}} \times Y^{q'}
    =
    (X \times Y)^A \cap (X^P \times Y^q)
    =
    Z^A \cap \mathrm{proj}_Y^{-1}(Y^q)
    \]
    it follows that $Z^Q$ is not only the $\pi$-pushforward of~$Z^A$ but also the $f$-pullback of $Y^Q$, where $f : Z^A \to Y^Q$ is the restriction of the projection map $\mathrm{proj}_Y : X^P \times Y^Q \to Y^Q$.
     
    This is a rare situation where an $f$-pullback has a good structure.
head: environment

label: ex:Dowker
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:Dowker}
    Let $R \subseteq I \times J$ be a binary relation between sets $I,J$. Define $A \leqslant \Delta(I) \times \Delta(J)$ by
    \[
    A = \{ (\sigma, \tau) \mid
    \sigma \in \Delta(I) ,\,
    \tau \in \Delta(J) ,\,
    \sigma \times \tau \subseteq R
    \}
    \]
    and let $D_I = D_I(R)$ and $D_J = D_J(R)$
     
    denote the projections of $A$ onto $\Delta(I)$ and $\Delta(J)$.
     
    These simplicial complexes are the Dowker complexes~\cite{Dowker_1952} of the binary relation~$R$. It is not difficult to show that both projections
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    D_I
    &
    A
        \ar[l]
        \ar[r]
    &
    D_J
    }
    \]
    have contractible point fibers and therefore are homotopy equivalences by Proposition~\ref{prop:product-fiber}.
     
    This is Dowker's theorem in poset language.
     
    When $I,J$ are finite, we can realize this diagram as a diagram of CL-complexes in various ways. The following diagram incorporates the two realizations of~$A$ from Example~\ref{ex:prod-complexes}.
     
    All arrows are CL-maps and homotopy equivalences.
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    &
    |\mathrm{simp}(A)|^A
        \ar[dl]
        \ar[d]^{\xi}
        \ar[dr]
    \\
    |D_I|^{D_I}
    &
    |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^A
        \ar[l]
        \ar[r]
    &
    |D_J|^{D_I}
    }
    \]
    Note that $|\mathrm{simp}(A)|$ is the `{rectangle complex}' in Brun and Salbu's proof of Dowker's Theorem~\cite{Brun_Salbu_2022}, while $|\mathrm{prod}(A)|$ is the `{relational product}' in one of the proofs by Yoon~\cite{Yoon_2026}.
     
    A third option is to use pushforwards:
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^{D_I}
    &
    |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^{A}
        \ar[l]
        \ar[r]
    &
    |\mathrm{prod}(A)|^{D_J}
    }
    \]
    By Example~\ref{ex:product-fiber-CL}, it follows that this is a diagram of CL-complexes. From this point of view, Dowker's theorem holds because the posets $A, D_I, D_J$ are realizable by the same space.
head: environment
name: Dowker's theorem

title: Example
body_md:
The following lattices of closed sets are tame classes:

(1)
Subcomplexes of a simplicial complex or CW-complex.

(2)
Compact semi-algebraic subsets of~$\mathbb{R}^n$.

(3)
Compact definable subsets of~$\mathbb{R}^n$ in an o-minimal theory~\cite{vdDries_1998}.

(4) Finite unions of compact convex sets in~$\mathbb{R}^n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) is covered by Example~\ref{ex:LC}(1) and Proposition~\ref{prop:cf-subcomplexes}.

(2), (3) reduce to (1) by the triangulation theorem \cite[Chapter~8, (2.9)]{vdDries_1998}.

(4) follows from the theory of ANR spaces: a finite union of compact convex sets is an ANR space and a closed inclusion of ANR spaces is a cofibration \cite[A.6.3, A.6.6, A.6.7]{Fritsch_Piccinini_1990}.

label: def:good-cover
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:good-cover}
     We call $\mathcal{U}$ a \emph{good cover} (of~$U^{\mathrm{all}}$) if every $U^\sigma$ is contractible or empty.
head: environment

label: def:tame-cover
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:tame-cover}
    We call $\mathcal{U}$ a \emph{tame cover} if the elements of~$\mathcal{U}$ belong to some tame class~$\mathcal{T}$.
head: environment

label: prop:tame
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:tame}
    A family of subsets $\mathcal{U} = (U_i \mid i \in I)$ of a topological space  is a tame cover iff every $U_i$ is closed and $U^A \to U^B$ is a cofibration for all $A \subseteq B \subseteq \Delta(I)$ with $A,B$ finite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Indeed $\mathcal{U}$ is a tame cover iff the smallest lattice containing the elements of~$\mathcal{U}$ is a tame class. We can identify this smallest lattice as $\{U^A \mid \varnothing \ne A \subseteq \Delta(I), \, \text{$A$ finite} \}$. When is it a tame class? The elements are closed sets iff every $U_i$ closed. The inclusions are cofibrations iff $U^A \to U^B$ is a cofibration whenever $U^A \subseteq U^B$. Ostensibly this is a broader quantification than `for all $A \subseteq B$', but in fact it is not more general, because when $U^A \subseteq U^B$ we have $U^B = U^B \cup U^A = U^{B \cup A}$ so the inclusion $U^A \to U^B$ can be written as $U^A \to U^{B \cup A}$.

label: thm:nerve
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: nerve theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
The ${N}^{\mathrm{op}}$-system $(U^\sigma \mid \sigma \in N$) defines a CL-complex structure on~$U^{\mathrm{all}}$: it is separated because ${N}^{\mathrm{op}}_x = \{ \sigma \in N \mid x \in U^\sigma \}$ has the ${N}^{\mathrm{op}}$-smallest\footnote{Largest in $N$.} element $m(x) = \{ i \in I \mid x \in U_i \}$ for all $x \in U^{\mathrm{all}}$, cellular since $\mathcal{U}$ is good, and link-cofibrant since $\mathcal{U}$ is tame.
 
    Thus $U^{\mathrm{all}}$ realizes the homotopy type of ${N}^{\mathrm{op}}$. This is the same as the homotopy type of~$N$, which is realized by $|\mathrm{Nerve}(\mathcal{U})|$.
head: environment

label: prop:nerve-natural
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: nerve theorem naturality

title: Remark
body_md:
It follows from
     
    the statement of
     
    Proposition~\ref{prop:nerve-natural}
     
    that if $\beta: I \to J$ is another function such that $f(U_i) \subseteq V_{\beta(i)}$ for all $i \in I$, then $|\phi_\alpha|, |\phi_\beta| : |N_{\mathcal{U}}| \to |N_{\mathcal{V}}|$ are homotopic. What matters, then, is the existence of~$\alpha$ and not what specific $\alpha$ is chosen.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We factor the diagram into three squares, where each of the eight objects is a CL-complex and each of the eight arrows is a CL-map.
    \[
    \xymatrix{
    U^{\mathrm{all}}
        \ar[r]
        \ar[d]_-{f}
    &
    |\mathrm{ord}({N_{\mathcal{U}}}^{\mathrm{op}})|
        \ar@{=}[r]
        \ar[d]^-{|\mathrm{ord}({\phi_\alpha}^{\mathrm{op}})|}
    &
    |\mathrm{ord}(N_{\mathcal{U}})|
        \ar[r]
        \ar[d]^-{|\mathrm{ord}(\phi_\alpha)|}
    &
    |N_{\mathcal{U}}|
        \ar[d]^-{|\phi_\alpha|}
    \\
    V^{\mathrm{all}}
        \ar[r]
    &
    |\mathrm{ord}({N_{\mathcal{V}}}^{\mathrm{op}})|
        \ar@{=}[r]
    &
    |\mathrm{ord}(N_{\mathcal{V}})|
        \ar[r]
    &
    |N_{\mathcal{V}}|
    }
    \]
     
    The four horizontal arrows are $\mathrm{id}$-maps (with respect to the posets ${N_{\mathcal{U}}}^{\mathrm{op}}$, $N_{\mathcal{U}}$, ${N_{\mathcal{V}}}^{\mathrm{op}}$, $N_{\mathcal{V}}$).
     
    The left two vertical arrows are ${\phi_{\alpha}}^{\mathrm{op}}$-maps. The right two vertical arrows are $\phi_{\alpha}$-maps.
     
    Then the two paths around the left-hand square are both ${\phi_{\alpha}}^{\mathrm{op}}$-maps so they are homotopic to each other. Likewise the two paths around the right-hand square are both $\phi_{\alpha}$-maps so they are homotopic to each other. Thus the two outer squares commute up to homotopy.
     
    The middle square commutes because $\mathrm{ord}(\phi) = \mathrm{ord}({\phi}^{\mathrm{op}})$ for any poset map~$\phi$.

label: thm:multi-nerve
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Sheehy's multicover nerve theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $K$ is up-closed in~$\Delta(I)$, it follows that ${(K \cap N)}^{\mathrm{op}}$ is closed in ${N}^{\mathrm{op}}$ and therefore specifies a subcomplex of the CL-complex in Theorem~\ref{thm:nerve}. The underlying space of this subcomplex is
\[
\bigcup_{\sigma \in K \cap N} U^\sigma
\;=\;
\bigg[
\,
    \bigcup_{\sigma \in K \cap N} U^\sigma
\,
\bigg]
\,\cup\,
\bigg[
\,
    \bigcup_{\sigma \in K - N} \varnothing
\,
\bigg]
\;=\;
\bigcup_{\sigma \in K} U^\sigma
\;=\;
U^K
\]
which confirms the first assertion.

For the second assertion, we have a canonical homotopy equivalence
\[
\xymatrix{
U^K
    \ar[r]
&
|\mathrm{ord}({(K \cap N)}^{\mathrm{op}})|
    \ar@{=}[r]
&
|\mathrm{ord}(K \cap N)|
}
\]
where the first map is any continuous ${(K \cap N)}^{\mathrm{op}}$-map of CL-complexes. Since chains in the poset $K \cap N$ are the same thing as chains in the poset~$N$ whose elements belong to $K \cap N$, it follows that $\mathrm{ord}(K \cap N)$ is the specified induced subcomplex of $\mathrm{ord}(N)$.
head: environment

label: prop:multi-nerve-natural
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: multicover nerve theorem naturality

title: Proof
body_md:
We factor the diagram into two squares.
\[
\xymatrix{
U^K
    \ar[r]
    \ar[d]_-{f}
&
|\mathrm{ord}({(K \cap N_{\mathcal{U}})}^{\mathrm{op}})|
    \ar@{=}[r]
    \ar[d]^-{\text{\rm inclusion}}
&
|\mathrm{ord}(K \cap N_{\mathcal{U}})|
    \ar[d]^-{\text{\rm inclusion}}
\\
V^K
    \ar[r]
&
|\mathrm{ord}({(K \cap N_{\mathcal{V}})}^{\mathrm{op}})|
    \ar@{=}[r]
&
|\mathrm{ord}(K \cap N_{\mathcal{V}})|
}
\]
 
This can be read as a `subdiagram' (restriction to subobjects) of the left two squares of the diagram in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:nerve-natural} (special case $I = J$, $\alpha = \mathrm{id}_I$) so it, too, commutes up to homotopy.
